sentences.text: Gracilisuchus was an extinct genus of tiny pseudosuchians that lived during the Late Triassic in Argentina.
This single species, G. stipanicicorum, belongs to the clade Suchia, which sits close to the ancestry of crocodylomorphs.
The largest known skull measures slightly over 9 cm in length, while the longest femur found is roughly 8 cm.
Its eye socket contained a scleral ring where ossicles touched without overlapping, and a small triangular postparietal bone was present in the skull. The neck region possessed eight vertebrae.
The lower end of the upper arm bone was 2.5 times wider than its shaft.
Two rows of bony plates called osteoderms ran from behind the skull over the neck and torso.
This animal differed from other rauisuchians by lacking an ossification at the back of the top of the skull and a fenestra between the premaxilla and maxilla.
For a time, this creature was considered a dinosaur.
Scientists think it might have been capable of running upright on its hind legs.
Alfred Romer first described both the genus and the species in 1972.
He published these descriptions in the journal Breviora that same year.
The fossils were discovered in the Los Chañares Formation within the Cuyo region of La Rioja Province, Argentina.
The holotype specimen, which is the specific example the species is based on, is now kept at the Museum of Paleontology at the National University of La Rioja under the number PULR 08.
The species name G. stipanicicorum honors the work of Pedro and Maria Stipanicic regarding the stratigraphy and paleobotany of the Triassic period.
It was a small predator whose diet consisted mainly of insects and small vertebrates.
Remains of Gracilisuchus and other tetrapods were found preserved within carbonate concretions in the rock.
Romer originally classified Gracilisuchus as a clear relative of Ornithosuchus based on skull and skeletal similarities.
Arthur Cruickshank later removed Gracilisuchus from Ornithosuchidae because it possessed a "crocodile-normal" ankle joint unlike other members of that family.
Brinkman tentatively placed Gracilisuchus closer to crocodile-line archosaurs like Erythrosuchidae and Rauisuchidae rather than Ornithosuchids.

Phylogenetic analysis recovered Gracilisuchus as a member of Suchia, defined by a "crocodile-normal" ankle and other traits. Paul Sereno removed Gracilisuchus from Ornithosuchids in 1991 and used it to define the contents of the group Suchia.
In 1994, Lars Juul placed Gracilisuchus inside Paracrocodylomorpha as the sister taxon of Postosuchus.
A 2004 analysis by Benton found Gracilisuchus to be the sister taxon of the Phytosauria.
A 2014 analysis by Richard Butler named a group containing Gracilisuchus, Turfanosuchus, and Yonghesuchus as Gracilisuchidae.
It is now considered a sister taxon to the Crocodylomorpha.
It lived in the middle Triassic, during the Anisian and Ladinian stages, approximately 240 to 235 million years ago.
Its time range is estimated from 241.464 to 237 million years ago during the Ladinian.
Uranium-lead dating of Chañares deposits in 2016 indicated an early Carnian age of 236 to 234 million years.
Romer debated the dinosaur classification of ornithosuchids, citing basal archosaur traits like the closed acetabulum and osteoderms in Gracilisuchus.
Scientists have not reached a consensus on the evolutionary relationships between Gracilisuchus and other crurotarsans.
Romer initially reconstructed Gracilisuchus as a facultative biped, though this interpretation was based on material later reassigned.
